A hard left bend where the water tears in from the right, slides fast and glassy round the outside cut bank furred with dripping moss, and rushes out left between two roots, a single grey pebble rearing up mid-channel like a cliff-face with a dead-calm eddy hiding in its shadow, the inside bar a pale crescent of clean sand.

The channel squeezes between two sandstone slabs, the flow above drawn into long oily pleats, then bursts out below in a boiling white fan into a wide copper-bedded pool, a strand of watercress bridging the gap overhead like a low rope-bridge, the deep side dark under the left overhang, the right side bright and knee-deep over yellow gravel.

Water pouring in from the upper left over a shallow riffle broken into a dozen small white crests on pebble backs, then collecting itself and sweeping right into a single deep groove under a clay bank bristling with root-hairs, the right side a bare gravel shelf so pale it almost glows, the bed visible and golden under barely a finger of moving water.

A flooded hollow among four great roots arching in from the left, the current braiding between them in bright separate threads, one thread deep amber, one nearly white where it catches air, joining again at the right-hand gap into a single purposeful tongue, the near side furred with duckweed that the current peels back in a long green comma at every surge.

The stream splitting round a hump of bright-green moss, the left channel deep and urgent and the right channel shallow enough to show every stone clearly through it, both arms tumbling back together beyond in a small boiling reunion, a single fallen oak leaf pinned against the moss island's upstream face, wide as the whole island and slowly drinking.

Water rushing in from the top right, breaking white over a low ridge of packed gravel, then calming into a smooth dark chute along the left bank under an overhang of clay and root, the right bank a long tongue of pale silt laid down in clean parallel ridges by the last flood, the bed shifting from dark mud left to bright pebble right.

A slow bend carrying the water in from the left wall, the outside bank a sheer face of dark wet soil laced with thin roots, the inside a broad bright gravel spit shelving gently under glass-clear water, one bulrush stem rising from the shallows taller than the whole picture's sky, its brown head level with the top of the frame.

The low step of a fallen alder twig spanning the channel, water piling and then folding over it in one smooth green tongue, dropping into a churning white skirt below, a deep still slot cut along the right bank in the twig's shadow, the left bank a gentle mud ramp printed with small paired bird tracks descending to the water's edge.

A narrow neck between two flint stones opening into a broad still reach, the water above the neck pulled into long stretched lines as it accelerates, breaking apart below into slow rolling boils that travel the full width of the pool, the right bank a tall wall of tangled root, the left bank open and gravelled with rounded stones each standing as high as a twig mast.

The current swings in hard from the right, undercuts a steep mossy bank on the far side eating at its base in a slow dark curl, and leaves a long still crescent of slack water along the near side where a raft of spinning sycamore keys has collected, the bed under the fast water dark and unreadable, the bed under the slack water bright ochre.

A shallow diagonal riffle crossing the frame from upper-left to lower-right, the water thin and fast and broken into overlapping white chevrons over small pebble backs, the left bank standing high with a wall of watercress rising like a dense green cliff, the right bank a bare swept gravel bar, one amber snail shell resting on it like a round tower.

Water threading in from the left between two arching tree roots that frame the entry like a gate, the channel immediately deepening and darkening, the far right bank a sheer face of rust-red clay, the near bank a gentle slope of dark silt where a feather lies half-submerged, the current drawing the feather's vane slowly sideways in a long arc.

A chute dropping in steeply from the upper right, the water white and loud at entry, spreading and slowing as it hits a wide flat pool, the surface of the pool riffled at the entry and glass-smooth ten lengths downstream, the right wall a sheer root-and-clay cliff, the left a long low bank of soft mud where the disturbed silt swirls in lazy pale threads.

The stream entering from the top left over a gravel bed so bright the water above it seems lit from below, bending right around a low island of packed dark mud and a single tuft of reed, the left channel deep and urgent, the right barely covering the stones, a mayfly resting on a mid-stream pebble with wings upright like two tall sails.

A bend under an overhang of roots so dense the water runs in their shadow, the current pressed hard to the right bank which is sheer and dark and wet, the left side opening into a bright still backwater barely connected to the main flow, its surface printed with the shadows of leaves moving high above, the bed shifting from black silt to clean white sand.

Water piling up against a single large flint mid-channel, splitting left and right with a small standing wave on its upstream face, the left branch deep and fast and the right branch frothing over a gravel shelf, both reuniting below the stone in a boiling seam, a fallen beech leaf plastered against the stone's face, its veins pressed flat and bright as copper wire.

A slow gentle bend, water entering from the upper right as a smooth dark surface, the outside bank a tall steep wall of green-furred soil, the inside a gradual gravel shelf sloping into the shallows, the current showing as long pale scratches on the dark surface, and a single root arching from the left bank all the way to mid-stream, dripping steadily into the flow.

The channel pinched between a clay spur jutting from the left and a root mass from the right, the water above the pinch piling up visibly, its surface humped and taut, pouring through the gap in a single fast rope, spreading into a wide calm reach below where the bed is pale gravel scattered with small dark stones like a scatter of little islands.

Water rushing in from the left, hitting a broad flat stone that angles it sharply downward into a short steep drop, the falling water punching a dark hole in the pool below and sending white rings outward across it, the far bank a gentle curve of pale silt, the near bank a vertical cut of dark root-threaded earth, one dandelion seed drifting across the whole still pool.

A long reach angling across the picture between two very different walls, the left bank a sheer wet face of compressed leaf-litter and root, the right a broad gravel spit studded with rounded pebbles each standing clear of the water's surface like a cluster of grey domes, the current hugging the left wall in a dark fast thread, the right side barely moving over bright stone.

The stream sliding in from the right under a low arch of bent reed stems, the arch so low the fast surface water brushes it, entering a wide pool where the current loses itself in slow revolving eddies, the left bank a wall of tree root with dark slots between each root, the right bank open and bright, the pool floor mapped in clear patches of sand and gravel.

Water breaking over a low transverse ridge of packed pebbles, the upstream face glassy and domed, the downstream face white and broken, settling into a deep amber run along the right bank under an overhang of moss, the left bank a pale mud ledge where the imprint of a heron's three-toed foot is pressed clean and deep into the silt.

A flooded stretch where the banks have vanished under the water, tree roots rising from it along one side like the pillars of a drowned hall, the current threading between them in quick bright lines, one backwater on the left perfectly still and dark, a fern frond drooping until its tip trails in the current and makes a small persistent V-wake in the flow.

The fast thread of current entering from the upper left in a tight rope of dark water, sweeping across to the lower right where it vanishes under a fringe of overhanging grass, the centre of the channel broken by two pebbles standing in close company, each sending a long smooth tail of calmer water downstream, the gravel bed between them bright and gold and readable through the thin fast water.

Water pouring in from the top between two roots and immediately spreading into a broad shallow fan over a pebble bed, every pebble breaking the surface into a small white crest, the crests overlapping across the whole width, the right bank a steep moss wall, the left bank open and low, a fallen hazelnut shell resting on the gravel of the shallows and standing over the shallow water like a boulder.

The channel cuts in hard from the left under a clay overhang bearded with wet moss, swings across fast and glassy, and slides out right between two gravel shelves, the bed showing amber straight through — a single acorn cup rolling along the bottom like a dropped millstone, the outside curve boiling white where the bank undercuts.

Water pours in from the upper left down a smooth green tongue over a twig-step, breaks into churning white below, then flattens and widens out toward the lower right, the far bank a wall of packed roots and the near side a long pale gravel ramp — a mayfly resting on a root wide as a rowing fae, wings folded flat.

The stream threads in from the right through a narrow gap between two mossy stones — the water drawn into long oily lines above and boiling in a white curl below — then opens left into a broad still pool, the floor gold gravel, a fallen birch leaf spinning slow in the eddy along the left wall like a raft becalmed.

A flooded hollow enters from the upper right, the current braiding between great arching roots in bright plaited lines, one backwater along the left furred thick with duckweed, and the main flow bending away to the lower left under a fern frond that arches the entire width like a vaulted roof — a water-snail shell on the gravel big as a boulder.

The riffle slides in from the top left diagonally, breaking white over a dozen pebble backs, the bed bright and stony under a finger of water, a wall of watercress standing thick along the right like a dense forest, and a bare gravel spit curving in low from the left — a single pebble midstream rising taller than any mast above the broken water.

A deep channel enters left under a sheer cut bank, the water sliding fast and almost black in the shadow there, then sweeps right across a bright gravel shelf barely deep enough to wet a hull — the shelf side lit gold, the cut-bank side dark — a strand of watercress trailing its roots across the narrows like a low rope bridge.

The stream bends in sharply from the right, pinches through a gap where a grey boulder-pebble stands mid-channel splitting the flow into two white tongues, and the two threads rejoin and run off left in a broad pale slide over a flat sandy bed — moss packed tight on the right bank, bare clay bank crumbling away on the left.

Water enters upper right down a chute between packed tree roots, clear and quick, pours into a wide dark pool, the surface rocking with slow rings, the bed invisible below the green shadow — on the left a low mud shelf with the pressed prints of small bird feet along the edge, and one fallen oak leaf beached there wide as three hulls.

The channel comes in from the left along one deep mossy wall, the water drawn into long smooth lines, swings round a tight bend and exits right down a shallow gravel run that breaks the surface into small white riffles — a bulrush rising from the right bank taller than any mast above the fleet, its velvet head shedding a slow drift of floss.

A still pool receives the current from the upper left through a gap between two stones, the inflow a bright white boil that fans out and quiets across the pool, the floor gold sand, and the water leaves lower right drawn thin and fast above a gravel lip — on the right a soft mud bank, on the left open water with an oak leaf turning.

The stream enters from upper right, slides fast and glassy round a hard bend under a cut bank of pale clay, the surface unbroken on the outside, shelving off right into bright amber gravel on the inside — tree roots cross overhead forming a dark arch — a single grey pebble standing in the shallows on the inside bend tall as a boulder, pinning foam.

Water braids in from the left between the humped backs of three pebbles standing like sea stacks, turns white and busy over each one, then collects into a single quiet run heading out lower right, the right bank a steeply mossy wall dripping, the left a flat bar of pale gravel, and a moth wing caught on the first pebble trembling in the flow.

The channel squeezes in from upper left between a root buttress and a hanging shelf of moss, the water fast and dark through the squeeze, then widens and slows heading right, the floor showing pale gravel, a small still eddy turning on the right behind the root — a hazelnut shell lodged in the eddy spinning steady as a wheel, too heavy to move on.

Current enters left along a steep root-hung bank, threads through a flooded gap between two root arches and exits right, the right side a wide shallow shelf of pebbles in bright amber light, the flow between them thin and clear — a single fern frond arching from the left bank out over the whole channel like a ceiling, dripping along its whole length.

A shallow riffle enters from upper right, the water thin and bright over flat gravel, breaks into small white crowns over pebble backs, and deepens suddenly as it turns out lower left along a mossy cut bank where the root of a great tree grips the clay — a blackthorn petal floating down the riffle face-up, broad as the channel is wide, unstuck and spinning.

The stream slides in from the right in one fast glassy tongue, splits round a small island of bright moss mid-channel — the left branch deep and quick, the right one barely covering the stones — and the two braid together and exit left in a broad riffled run, one whole fallen alder leaf bridging the left channel at the island's tip like a plank.

Water pours in upper left, runs fast and smooth along a sheer clay wall, the surface oily and dark near the wall, turns right in a wide curve and flattens out over a pale sandy shelf where the bed shows clear through a hand's depth — a clump of watercress rooted at the bend stands along the right bank like a small crowded forest.

The channel enters right through a narrow slot between two grey stone faces, the water loud and white at the slot, then fans into a quiet pool, surface rocking, and drains away left between gravel bars, the bar on the right built higher and dry with a fringe of moss at its edge, the bar on the left submerged and only showing as a gold shape below.

A chute drops in from upper left between close-packed stones, the water green and smooth above, white and broken below, and the broken water spreads and quiets heading right across a broad sandy floor — the right bank a wall of packed roots, the left side open with a slow eddy turning — an oak-gall resting on the left eddy floor, round as a boulder.

The stream bends in from the right under arching root-fingers that cross overhead, the current fast and braided, hits a standing pebble mid-channel and splits white on both sides, comes back together and runs out lower left into a still reach — the left bank a cut face of wet clay, the right a low gravel point — a pine needle caught upright on the pebble, shivering.

Water enters from upper right down a long glassy run over smooth flat stone, the bed showing copper and amber through the clear depth, hits a twig-dam spanning the channel and pours over in one smooth green lip into white froth below, then exits lower left — the left bank a steep moss wall, the right a soft mud shelf holding the hollowed print of a heron's foot.

The channel comes from the left fast and narrow between a wall of clay hung with roots and a gravel bar, pinches through, then widens right into a pool where the current dies in long slow curves — the pool floor bright with white sand — a single bulrush on the right bank rises taller than any vessel's mast, its reflection lying straight down the still water.

A wide shallow riffle enters upper left, the water thin and busy over pebble backs, bright broken white, and the right side deepens as it goes — the left staying shallow gravel, the right carving into a mossy undercut bank — the channel exits lower right through a root arch, and a cluster of watercress on the left stands bank-to-bank wide enough to hide the sky above it.

Current enters from the right through a flooded gap between root buttresses, threading in three bright lines between the dark wood, then spreads into a deep backwater on the left — surface still, furred at the edges with duckweed — while the main run curves away lower right over amber gravel, and a snail on the left wall leaves a bright trail across the clay above the waterline.

The stream slides in from upper left along a deep wall of overhanging roots, the surface fast and dark on that side, and shelves away right into pale gravel so shallow the stones break the surface — a fallen oak leaf has snagged on the first stone midchannel, as wide as the shallow shelf, rocking on the current, and the water pours white round both its tips.

Water rushes in right through a gap where two grey pebbles face each other like gateposts — white and loud between them — then calms fast into a broad pool heading left, the floor gold clear through, a raft of tiny bubbles riding the surface out from the gap in a long white tongue — the right bank mossy and dripping, the left a bare pale shelf of sand.

The channel enters upper left down a gravel riffle, bright and noisy, deepens at the centre where a mossy stone parts the water into two white arcs, and the arcs rejoin and slide out right in a smooth dark run below the stone — the left bank high and root-hung casting shadow, the right bank low and lit, a hawthorn berry bobbing on its grass line at the turn.

A narrow chute enters from the right between a root face and a grey stone, the water in it drawn fast and smooth into long oily lines, then breaks into foam as it hits the pool, and the pool drains away slowly left over a low lip of flat stone, the floor pale, the left bank a mud slope with cress crowding the edge, the right bank open bright water.

The stream enters left fast under a sheer moss wall, sweeps across and slows as it meets a gravel bank building up from the right, the inside curve amber and lit, the outside dark and undercut — a fern frond grows from the left bank and arches out clear over the channel, each pinnule holding a bright bead of water that drops into the current below.

Current enters upper right through a gap in a thatch of crossing root-fingers, the water loud and braided, settles into a quiet wide run heading lower left over bright sandy bottom — the left bank a gravel spit built low and open, the right a clay wall with moss in the cracks — a single grey pebble standing in the shallows midstream, foam piled against it like a breaking wave.

The channel cuts hard left under a steep clay bank riddled with root-holes, the water pressed flat and fast on that side, glassy and dark, then fans out right across a broad gravel shelf where it runs shin-deep and broken, one fallen oak leaf pinned broadside against an upstream pebble, trembling in the current like a buckled raft.

A chute between two moss-shouldered stones drives the water down into a pool that spreads wide and breathes out slow, the bed showing clean gold gravel through the stillness, the left bank a sheer wet wall of liverwort and the right a pale gravel spit, a single bulrush rising from the spit taller than any mast the fleet could dream of carrying.

The stream bends hard right, the outside bank a hanging wall of root-lace dripping into the fast lane, the inside shelving away into a bright stony shallows where the water barely covers the bed, a watercress bank standing along the far curve like a dense green forest, its stems thick as tree trunks at this reading of the world.

Water pours over the low dam of a fallen twig in one smooth green tongue, breaking into white froth below, the slot behind the twig holding a deep still shadow, the near bank a soft mud shelf tilted gently in and printed all over with the toeprints of some wading bird, each print a broad crater at fae measure.

The channel splits around a small moss island, the left arm deep and urgent and the right one thin and bright over white pebbles, the two currents rejoining in a boil of crossed lines beyond the island's tail, a strand of watercress trailing from the island's downstream tip and crossing the right channel like a low bridge the hulls must duck beneath.

A flooded hollow opens between four great roots arching up from the water like the piers of some immense old bridge, the current threading between them in bright braided ropes, a backwater on the left gone perfectly still and filmed with green duckweed, a snail shell resting on the gravel in the deep centre, round and pale as a dropped millstone.

The water runs fast and shallow diagonally left to right across a wide stony riffle, breaking white over a dozen pebble backs that stand up like reef crags, the left bank a sheer cut of dark earth with grass roots dangling, the right bank open and low, a single grey river pebble rising from the far right edge boulder-tall above the racing hulls.

A long oily tongue of water is drawn down into a narrow gap between a mossy root on the left and a pale stone on the right, the surface above the gap smoothed into trembling glass, below it boiling and white and wide, the left bank root-dark and overhanging, the right open, a fern frond reaching far out over the gap from above.

The stream slides fast along the left side under a clay cliff where the bank has sheared clean away, then slows across a broad shelf of ginger gravel on the right, one mayfly hovering just above the surface in the slow water, its wings as wide as a racing hull is long, its shadow crossing the bright bed below like a passing cloud.

A hard outside bend presses all the speed into the right channel beneath an undercut bank where the earth hangs over in a dark shelf, the inside curving away into a pale gravel crescent that barely holds a finger of water, an oak leaf drifting down the fast side large enough to carry three boats on its back with room to spare.

The current threads through a flooded root-maze, each root a curved stone bridge at this scale, bright braided lines of fast water winding between pools of deep amber stillness, the left side open sky above open water, the right side roofed entirely by a broad fern frond arching from bank to bank, its shadow striping the water dark and pale in bands.

Water spills left to right over a long shallow step of compacted silt, the lip smoothed into a single unbroken curve, the plunge below it white and loud, the pool beyond spreading wide and quiet, left bank a wall of exposed roots coiled like rope, right bank a gentle mud beach, a hazelnut shell half-buried in the mud big as a boulder at the waterline.

The channel enters from the upper left in a fast glassy run, hits a wall of clay on the right bank and turns sharply downward, the outside of the bend dark and undercut, the inside a bright sickle of fine gravel, the current peeling off the clay in long curling eddies, a seed-pod the shape of a boot spinning slowly in the biggest eddy.

Two stones stand close together near the right bank, forcing the whole river through the gap between them, the water above drawn into smooth accelerating lines, the water below standing up briefly in a brief clear ridge before falling into foam, left bank open and gravelly, right bank steep and root-hung, a single acorn cap caught on the lip of the gap, rocking.

The stream runs over a long clean riffle from upper right to lower left, the bed all white and amber pebbles showing clear through a thin bright skin of water, each pebble a boulder to the fleet racing above it, the left bank a dense stand of watercress crowding the edge, the right bank a bare pale spit of sand curving gently outward.

A deep still pool gathers in the lower half of the picture, fed from the upper right by a fast narrow run between two clay walls, the transition from fast to still marked by a spreading fan of surface lines, the pool floor all clean gold gravel, the left bank hung with roots, the right bank low and open, a wren feather drifting down the surface.

The water enters upper left tight and fast between a root-wall and a pale stone, fans right across a wide pool paved with bright pebbles, each one a boulder-back breaking the surface or looming large and dark beneath, a frond of duckweed riding the main current like a slow green island, the left bank sheer cut clay, the right bank a long low gravel bar.

A chute opens suddenly from a root-roofed tunnel on the left into brilliant open water on the right, the current shooting out and curving right in a long smooth arc before settling, the tunnel bank root-dark and dripping, the far bank a low mossy shelf just above water level, a strand of milkweed floss snagged across the chute's mouth, trembling hard in the rush.

The stream runs hard along the right wall, that bank a sheer liverwort cliff veined with seeping water, the current shearing away from it in long fast lines, then crossing the full width to exit lower left across a gravel crossing where the water breaks pale and thin over the stones, a small moss island holding the centre, splitting the last of the race into two.

Water pours right to left over the curved back of a half-buried pebble, the upstream face of the stone holding a smooth glassy pillow of water, the downstream face a white cascade into a pool the colour of dark tea, left bank an open silt shelf, right bank a tangle of fine roots hanging into the current, a fallen birch seed spinning in the eddy below.

The channel narrows from left to right under a clay overhang on the left that drips steadily into the fast lane, the right bank shelving away in pale gravel to where the water runs clear and barely moving, a watercress stem falling right across the channel near the lower edge, its leaves holding small silver bubbles on their undersides like a row of lanterns.

A flooded rut between two root-buttresses carries the water from the upper right in a bright quick braid, the left buttress rising like a cliff, the right buttress lower and mossy, the current threading the gap and spreading into a wider reach below, a flat oval pebble lying on the bed at the exit, pale and enormous through the clear water above it.

The outside of a wide left bend holds deep fast water against a bank of packed clay and hanging grass, the inside curved into a long white gravel spit where the water runs barely deep enough to float a shell, a single dried oak gall lodged against the clay bank on the fast side, the current parting round it as though round a fixed stone pier.

Water slides down a shallow slope from upper right, hits a transverse ridge of embedded pebbles and breaks into a dozen white threads, each thread finding its own line through the gaps in the ridge, the left bank a wall of fern roots, the right bank open silt, a mayfly resting on the largest pebble of the ridge, its wings catching the current, rocking gently.

The stream enters tight from the right between a steep root-wall and the side of a large pale stone, rounds the stone on the left in a fast curl, and opens into a wide pool below, the pool perfectly still at the edges but still moving at the centre in slow oily coils, the stone's upstream face silvered with a smooth water-pillow, its downstream face foaming white.

A shallow crossing runs from upper left to lower right over a bright amber gravel bed, the water only a finger deep and clear as glass, the bed every colour of stone visible straight through, the left bank a dense green mat of liverwort at the water's edge, the right bank undercut clay, a fallen sycamore key resting on the gravel like a strange wide-winged thing beached.

The current threads between two mossy root-arches rising from the bed like paired gateposts, squeezing fast through the gap and fanning out below into a wide quiet reach, the left bank overhung with grass leaning far out into the picture, the right bank sheer and root-veined, a strand of moss trailing from the right-hand root-arch across half the channel into the current below.

The water runs into the picture from the upper left between a clay bank and a flat stone shelf on the right, the stone shelf nearly at water level and bright with wet algae, the current fast above the shelf and still below it in a wide pool, a rowanberry bobbing on a grass tether where the fast water meets the still, tugging hard against the line.

A long diagonal riffle crosses from the right bank to the left, the water breaking into white caps over every pebble back in the crossing, the right bank a high root-wall from which one thick root descends to the waterline and into it, the left bank a low open gravel beach, a snail shell resting on that beach at the water's edge, round and pale and enormous.

The channel splits left and right around a low tongue of packed silt and fine gravel, the left arm carrying the main current deep and fast, the right arm shallow and slow over bright stones, the two arms closing again in a boil of meeting lines, a whole fallen alder leaf bridging the narrows between island-tip and right bank, its surface dimpled by the water rushing beneath.

The current slices in from the left under a steep clay cut bank threaded with roots, swings hard right, and drains out through a gap between two stones, the water pulled into long oily cables above the gap and bursting white below it, a single clover head revolving in the eddy on the shelving gravel side.

A chute between two mossy stones fires the stream from the top-left corner into a wide still pool, the floor showing copper-gold gravel straight through the glass, one fallen oak leaf drifting across the pool as wide as three boats abreast, a backwater on the left side furred edge-to-edge with bright duckweed.

The channel bends left under a hanging curtain of root-hair, the outside water fast and black, the inside shelving into a bright gravel spit, and one grey pebble rising from the middle of the bend tall as a cliff, the stream boiling white on its upstream face and trailing a long smooth wake behind it.

The stream drops over the low step of a water-logged twig crossing the whole channel, pouring in one smooth jade tongue into froth, a deep undercut slot running along the far bank under packed earth and root, a soft silt shelf on the near side pressed with the paired prints of a wood pigeon.

Water threads in from the upper right between arching tree roots, braiding into bright distinct lines across a flooded hollow, a still backwater on the left holding a single upright bulrush rising taller than any mast, the right bank a bare steep wall of dark peat with one rootlet dangling into the current like a rope.

A shallow riffle runs diagonally from the top-left to the bottom-right, the bed entirely visible through a finger of water, broken into a dozen small white crests over pebble backs, a dense bank of watercress standing on the left like a pillared forest, and a bare pale gravel spit cutting in from the right.

The channel enters top-right, swings round a low island of bright moss, splits into a fast deep left arm and a shallow rattling right arm, and closes again at the bottom of the picture, one strand of watercress lying across the narrows below the island like a low fallen bridge between the two rejoining flows.

Current slides in from the left along a deep channel cut tight against a sheer root-wall, the surface there flat and fast and dark, then the bed rises abruptly to a gravel shelf on the right where the water shallows to almost nothing, a mayfly resting on the surface of the deep side large as a heron.

The stream pours through a flooded hollow between four great roots entering from the top and leaving between the bottom two, the current dividing and rejoining in braided copper threads, a snail shell sitting on the gravel floor below the water as big as a boulder, moss covering the root walls on both sides in dense green.

A hard left-to-right bend, the water on the outside scouring the bank to bare dark peat and swinging fast and glassy, the inside piled with rounded pebbles standing out of the shallows, the largest one a grey dome the size of a roundhouse, a fern frond arching over the outer bank like a vast roof.

The current runs in from the top between a root-ridged left bank and a low right bank of open sand, accelerates through a narrow slot and blows out into a pool at the bottom, the surface above the slot drawn into long smooth parallel oily lines, a fallen birch leaf spinning slowly in the pool's far eddy.

Water slides in from the left, strikes a flat-faced stone and deflects right and downward, boiling white directly behind the stone and settling fast into a dark run along the steep mossy bank, the far side a gentle slope of clean gravel where the froth arrives in slow pale islands and dissolves.

A riffle enters upper-left over a pale gravel bed, the water breaking white across the whole width, then gathers into one dark tongue along the right bank where a cut root overhangs, and exits lower-right, the left bank a low spit of fine sand printed with the star-foot of a wading bird.

The stream splits round a long moss island, the left fork deep and hurrying under an arch of packed root, the right fork thin as glass over pale stone, one whole fallen oak leaf bridging the right fork from bank to island as wide as three boats, the two channels meeting again in a swirl of opposing dimples.

Current enters upper-right between steep peat walls and drops over a submerged ridge of packed gravel, the surface piling into a low standing wave before flattening into a wide pool, the pool floor brilliant gold-and-white under clear water, a clump of watercress standing on the left wall of the pool like a dense canopy.
